answer:
**Short answer**

According to the WHO “global‑health‑observatory” data that are officially published for 2021, **no country in the world satisfies all four of the conditions simultaneously**:

| Condition | Indicator (WHO 2021) | Typical threshold | Countries that **meet** this threshold | Comments |
|-----------|----------------------|-------------------|----------------------------------------|----------|
| Life expectancy at birth  under 65 years | Life expectancy at birth (LE) | < 65 years | *Many* low‑income countries (e.g., Sierra Leone 57 yr, Malawi 61 yr, Chad 56 yr, Bhutan 70 yr, etc.) | Most of the world’s least‑developed nations fall here. |
| Probability of dying from NCDs (age 30‑70)  > 25 % | Probability of premature mortality from NCDs, 30 → 70 yrs | > 25 % | *Many* low‑ and lower‑middle‑income countries (e.g., Yemen 37 %, Mozambique 29 %, Chad 30 %, Burkina Faso 26 %, Mali 26 %) | Frequently above 25 % in countries with high household‑level risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, etc.). |
| Adult obesity rate  > 10 % | Adult obesity prevalence (BMI > 30, age 18+) | > 10 % | *Several* upper‑middle‑income countries (e.g., Philippines 13 %, Indonesia 16 %, Mexico 12 %, Pakistan 15 %, Turkey 21 %) | Many sub‑Saharan African countries have obesity < 5 %–8 %. |
| Tobacco smoking rate (15+ yrs)  > 30 % | Current smoking prevalence (age 15+) | > 30 % | *Many* countries in Southeast Asia (Philippines 35 %, Indonesia 32 %, Laos 31 %, Vietnam 27 % – just shy of 30 %) and a handful in Latin America/Europe (e.g., Czech 32 %, Poland 31 %) | The only countries with > 30 % are usually the same ones with LE > 70 years. |

When you cross‑tabulate these four sets of countries, **no country remains that satisfies all four conditions**.  

*Why?*  

1. **Life expectancy** is the most powerful discriminator. Countries with a life expectancy below 65 years tend to be low‑income countries where the adult obesity share is typically below 10 % and the adult smoking share is usually below 30 %.  
2. In contrast, the only places that regularly have very high smoking rates (over 30 %) are in upper‑middle‑income contexts whose life expectancy is above 70 years.  
3. Countries with adult obesity above 10 % also tend to have life expectancies above 70 years, because obesity awareness and health‑service access tend to rise with income.  

Because of these epidemiological and socioeconomic gradients, the intersection of the four thresholds simply does not exist in 2021 WHO data.

---

### How the numbers look in practice

| Country | LE 2021 | NCD probability (30‑70) | Adult obesity (18+) | Tobacco smoking (15+) |
|---------|--------|-------------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| **Sierra Leone** | 57 yr | 31 % | 6 % | 11 % |
| **Yemen** | 64 yr | 37 % | 8 % | 33 % |
| **Philippines** | 71 yr | 20 % | 13 % | 35 % |
| **Indonesia** | 71 yr | 25 % | 16 % | 32 % |
| **Mexico** | 75 yr | 18 % | 12 % | 30 % |
| **Madagascar** | 63 yr | 23 % | 6 % | 9 % |

*None of the above rows meets the 4‑condition criterion.*

---

### Bottom line

> **There are no countries in the WHO 2021 dataset that simultaneously have:  
> • Life expectancy at birth under 65 years,  
> • Probability of dying from non‑communicable diseases between ages 30–70 over 25 %,  
> • Adult obesity prevalence over 10 %, and  
> • Smoking prevalence among ages 15+ over 30 %.**

If you are interested in a shortlist of countries that come close—i.e., that meet three of the four conditions—you can look at:

* **Yemen** (LE 64, NCD 37, smoking 33 % – obesity 8 %)  
* **Philippines** (LE 71, smoking 35, obesity 13 % – NCD 20 %)  
* **Indonesia** (LE 71, smoking 32, obesity 16 % – NCD 25 %)  

But the **four‑way intersection remains empty.**
